children: By Paulo Trevisani and Emese Bartha
Global government bond yields rose on Wednesday after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates as expected.

The central bank increased the benchmark federal-funds target range by a quarter point to between 3.75% and 4%, in the first rate hike since 2023. The majority of officials predicted one more uptick this year.

The two-year Treasury yield increased to 4.734% from 4.606% before the rate decision. The 10-year rose back to 5% from 4.945%. Yields also rose in Germany and Japan, partially reversing early declines.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh reinforced the institution's commitment to reduce inflation, adding that a confluence of factors is driving bond yields higher.

"I think part of the reason why we've seen over the course of 2026 long-term yields go up is the economy has strengthened," Warsh told reporters. Another reason is competition for capital from large corporations building up AI infrastructure.
A third one is geopolitics, as conflicts around the world put upward pressure on energy and food products that could "find their way into stores across the country," he said.
Warsh, however, stopped short of confirming that further tightening is coming, maintaining a higher level of uncertainty than bond investors are accustomed to.

"The history is clear that once the Fed begins raising rates, they do it multiple times, but the pattern is less clear about whether they will raise rates at consecutive meetings," Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management said in a note. He added that spread out hikes are more likely.
Brent oil prices fell 3% to $106.90 per barrel.
Markets price in a roughly 50-50 probability of a similar increase or hold at the next meeting in October, according to CME.
Jessica Coacci contributed to this article.
